styles.Narrator: a warm, curious nature-documentary narrator, calm and unhurried, clear diction, speaking English

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Bees never studied geometry. Yet every cell they build is a hexagon. Why a hexagon?
lines.style: opening hook, quietly amazed, the question lands with a small lift

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The comb is made of wax. And wax is expensive. A bee has to eat many pounds of honey, to make a single pound of wax.
lines.style: explaining, a little emphasis on how costly it is

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So here is the bee's problem. Store as much honey as possible, using as little wall as possible.
lines.style: setting up a puzzle, measured, clear

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A circle needs the least wall. But pack circles together, and gaps are left over.
lines.style: thoughtful, a slight letdown on the second half

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Regular shapes that cover a floor with no gaps? There are only three. Triangles. Squares. And hexagons.
lines.style: counting off the three shapes one by one, steady

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Give every cell the same area. Triangles need the most wall. Squares come second. Hexagons need the least.
lines.style: comparing, building to the winner on the last phrase

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Mathematicians wondered about this for over two thousand years. It was finally proven in nineteen ninety-nine. No shape beats the hexagon.
lines.style: telling a bit of history, impressed by how long it took

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It took humans more than two thousand years to prove it. The bees had it right all along.
lines.style: closing line, warm and wry, a small pause before the last phrase
